title: WHAT IF THE JESUS YOU’VE BEEN LOOKING AT IS NOT THE JESUS YOU’VE BEEN WORSHIPING?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE JESUS YOU’VE BEEN LOOKING AT IS NOT THE JESUS YOU’VE BEEN WORSHIPING?
The uncomfortable truth about pictures of Jesus, the Second Commandment, and the dangerous moment when a beautiful reminder becomes a substitute for the living Savior.
There is a picture of Jesus hanging on somebody’s wall tonight.
Maybe it is in a grandmother’s bedroom. Maybe it is above a family dining table. Maybe it is inside a church where generations have knelt, wept, confessed their sins, and begged God for mercy.
The painting shows a gentle face. Long hair. Compassionate eyes. Arms stretched wide.
A mother looks at it while praying for her rebellious son.
A grieving husband stares at it after burying his wife.
A young woman who has almost given up on life sees it and remembers that Jesus loves her.
And somewhere else, another Christian looks at that very same picture and says something that makes the entire room uncomfortable.
“That is a violation of the Second Commandment.”
Suddenly, what seemed like an innocent expression of devotion becomes a question of obedience.
One believer sees a reminder of grace.
Another sees a dangerous misrepresentation of God.
Both open their Bibles.
Both claim to honor Jesus.
And both cannot understand how the other could be so mistaken.
But here is the question that should disturb us more than the argument itself.
What if we have spent so much time defending our pictures of Jesus—or condemning someone else's—that we have forgotten to ask whether our hearts are truly surrendered to Him?
Before you defend the painting on your wall, or demand that someone remove theirs, there is something in Scripture we need to face.
Because this conversation is not ultimately about paint, canvas, carved wood, digital illustrations, or religious traditions.
It is about the holiness of God.
The authority of His Word.
The mystery of the incarnation.
And the terrifying possibility of being religiously devoted to something that is not actually the Lord.
God has already spoken about images. But have we listened carefully enough to understand what He said?

When the Lord delivered Israel from Egypt, He did not merely rescue them from slavery. He called them out of a world saturated with idols, where gods were represented through statues, carved figures, and images fashioned by human hands.
At Mount Sinai, God declared:

“You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them.”
— Exodus 20:4–5, ESV
The Hebrew word translated “carved image” is פֶּסֶל (pesel), referring to a carved or sculpted image, particularly in the context of idolatry.
Another important word is תְּמוּנָה (temunah), meaning a form, likeness, or representation.
And the command goes beyond making an object. It expressly forbids bowing down to such images or serving them.
This was not a minor instruction.
It was covenant faithfulness.
Israel belonged to the living God, not to gods they could manufacture, decorate, carry, or control.
But pay attention to something that is often overlooked.
The same God who prohibited idolatrous images later instructed Moses to make cherubim of gold over the mercy seat of the ark (Exodus 25:18–20).
He also commanded the construction of a bronze serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:8–9).
And Solomon’s temple contained carved cherubim, palm trees, and flowers (1 Kings 6:29).
So the biblical prohibition cannot simply mean that every artistic representation of a created thing is sinful.
God Himself authorized certain religious imagery.
But that does not settle whether images representing God—or specifically Jesus—may be used in Christian devotion.
That is where the question becomes more difficult.
Because the cherubim were not portraits of God.
The bronze serpent was not a representation of the divine nature.
And the presence of sacred art in the temple does not automatically establish permission to create devotional portraits of Christ.
We must not force Scripture to say more than it says.
Nor should we ignore what it plainly teaches.
There is another warning buried in Israel’s history.
And it is heartbreaking.
The bronze serpent was originally an instrument through which God brought healing when the Israelites looked toward it in obedient faith.
But centuries later, the people began burning incense to that same object.
King Hezekiah destroyed it.
Why?
Because something God had once used for good had become an object of corrupted devotion (2 Kings 18:4).
Think about that.
An object connected to a genuine act of God had become spiritually dangerous because of what people were doing with it.
The problem was no longer the serpent’s original purpose.
The problem was the worship it had begun to receive.
And that should make every Christian examine the heart.
Because even something associated with a true spiritual experience can become an idol when it receives the reverence that belongs to God alone.
A cross can become a superstition.
A church building can become an object of misplaced trust.
A pastor can become an untouchable authority.
A religious tradition can become more precious than obedience.
And yes, an image of Jesus can become an idol.
But we must also be careful not to conclude that every Christian who owns a painting of Jesus is necessarily worshiping that painting.
Scripture requires us to distinguish between what a person possesses, what a person intends, and what a person actually does.
Then we arrive at one of the most astonishing declarations in the New Testament.
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
— John 1:14, ESV
In Greek, the opening words are:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not an illusion.
Not a symbolic appearance.
Not a heavenly projection pretending to be human.
Flesh.
The eternal Son of God truly entered human history.
He was born of Mary.
He grew.
He ate.
He slept.
He experienced exhaustion.
He wept.
He was touched by human hands.
And He walked among people who could see His face.
This changes the conversation.
Because the Christian faith does not teach that Jesus was merely an invisible spirit.
Jesus Christ is one divine Person with two natures, truly God and truly man.
He possessed a real human body.
A real human face.
A real human appearance.
And yet the New Testament gives us no reliable physical description detailed enough to reconstruct His face.
We know His historical setting.
We know He was a Jewish man living in first-century Judea and Galilee.
But we do not know the exact shape of His eyes, the precise length of His hair, or the features that would make a modern portrait a verified likeness.
That familiar painting you grew up with?
It may be meaningful to you.
It may be beautiful.
But it is not a documented photograph of Jesus.
And we should never confuse artistic imagination with historical certainty.
Here is where faithful Christians have reached different conclusions.

Many Eastern Orthodox Christians defend the use of icons because the eternal Son truly became visible in the incarnation. They distinguish between worship, which belongs to God alone, and the honor shown to an icon, which they understand as directed toward the person represented.
The Second Council of Nicaea in AD 787 formally defended the veneration of icons while distinguishing it from the adoration owed to God alone.

Many Roman Catholics similarly distinguish between the worship owed to God and the relative honor given to sacred images. Catholic teaching maintains that the honor shown to an image is directed toward the person depicted, not toward the material object as a god.

Many Reformed Protestants, however, reject images of Christ used in worship and often reject all attempted portraits of Him. They argue that the Second Commandment forbids humanly devised representations of God, and that Christ's true humanity cannot be separated from His divine person.

Other Protestants permit non-worshipful illustrations of Jesus in teaching, children's books, historical art, or devotional settings, while rejecting prayer to images or treating them as sacred objects possessing spiritual power.
These are not insignificant differences.
They concern how Christians understand the Second Commandment, the incarnation, worship, and the authority of Scripture.
And they deserve serious examination, not insults.
But the most important thing is this:
No painting can reveal Jesus more truthfully than the Word of God.
An artist can imagine His facial expression.
Scripture reveals His character.
An artist can paint His hands.
Scripture tells us what those hands did.
An artist can portray His eyes.
Scripture tells us how He looked upon sinners with compassion, exposed hypocrisy, and confronted evil.
A painting may suggest His suffering.
The Gospel tells us why He suffered.
And that difference matters eternally.
Because the greatest danger is not merely imagining what Jesus looked like.
It is imagining a Jesus who never existed.
A Jesus who never confronts sin.
A Jesus who never calls anyone to repentance.
A Jesus who exists only to affirm our preferences.
A Jesus who never speaks about judgment, holiness, self-denial, or the narrow way.
A Jesus who makes us comfortable but never makes us new.
You can reject every religious picture in the world and still worship a false version of Christ in your imagination.
And you can own a painting of Jesus while genuinely trusting the biblical Savior, even if another sincere Christian disagrees with your judgment about the painting.
This is why the question must go deeper than the wall.
What does your heart believe about the Man portrayed there?
Because Jesus is not merely the gentle figure in religious artwork.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).
He is the One who said:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
— Mark 1:15, ESV
And repentance is not a decorative word.
The Greek verb μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) means “repent,” calling for a genuine turning of heart and life in response to God.
It is not merely feeling guilty for a few minutes.
It is not crying during worship and returning unchanged to cherished sin.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose grace makes forgiveness and transformation possible.
And perhaps that is where this conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easier to argue about an image of Jesus than to obey the words of Jesus.
It is easier to criticize someone's religious traditions than to forgive the person who wounded you.
It is easier to defend a sacred painting than to surrender the secret sin you have protected for years.
It is easier to debate the Second Commandment than to examine whether money, success, lust, pride, bitterness, or public approval has become your functional god.
An idol does not always have a face.
Sometimes it has a bank account.
Sometimes it has a notification sound.
Sometimes it is the applause you cannot live without.
Sometimes it is the relationship you refuse to surrender even though it is leading you away from Christ.
And sometimes it is the version of yourself you desperately want everyone to admire.
That is why the apostle John closes his first letter with a remarkably direct warning:
“Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”
— 1 John 5:21, ESV
He was writing to believers.
People who already knew the truth.
People who had heard about Jesus.
And still, they needed that warning.
So do we.
But there is something else we must not overlook.
Paul wrote:
“He is the image of the invisible God.”
— Colossians 1:15, ESV
The Greek word translated “image” is εἰκών (eikōn).
It means image or likeness, and in this passage it describes Christ's unique revelation of the invisible God.
This is not a statement that a painted icon is equivalent to Christ.
Nor does the verse, by itself, settle whether Christians may paint His human appearance.
Paul is declaring something infinitely greater.
Jesus Himself perfectly reveals the Father.
Not because an artist successfully captured His features.
But because He is the eternal Son.
As Jesus told Philip:
“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
— John 14:9, ESV
He was not saying that the Father has the same physical face as Jesus.
He was revealing the profound unity between the Son and the Father.
Jesus makes the Father known through His person, words, and works.
And here is the tragedy.
We can become so fascinated with how Jesus might have looked that we neglect what Jesus actually said.
We can spend hours arguing about portraits while leaving our Bibles closed.
We can surround ourselves with Christian imagery and remain strangers to prayer.
We can wear a cross around our neck while refusing to carry the cross of discipleship.
We can decorate our homes with verses about love while treating our families with cruelty.
We can fill our social media profiles with images of Christ while hiding a life that refuses His lordship.
And eventually we must ask ourselves:
Am I following Jesus?
Or am I merely surrounding myself with reminders of someone I refuse to obey?
That question is not meant to crush the struggling believer.
It is meant to awaken us.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that only spiritually successful people may approach God.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
People with histories they cannot erase.
People who have made idols out of relationships, ambition, religion, and even their own suffering.
People who have mistaken familiarity with Christianity for genuine fellowship with Christ.
People who have walked into church smiling while carrying shame nobody knows about.
People who have failed so many times that they wonder whether grace could possibly reach them again.
And if that describes you, listen carefully.
The answer is not to manufacture a more comforting image of Jesus.
The answer is to come to the real Jesus.
The One who received sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who called people to leave their sins.
The One who went willingly to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls the weary to Himself.
He does not need you to pretend that your heart is clean.
He calls you to repent and trust Him.
And He does not need a painter to make His mercy real.
His mercy was displayed at Calvary.
Consider the thief crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to commission sacred artwork.
No time to decorate a prayer room.
No religious achievements to present.
His life was collapsing.
His body was dying.
His guilt was real.
And yet he turned to Jesus and said:
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
— Luke 23:42, ESV
Jesus answered:
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”
— Luke 23:43, ESV
There was no image between that dying sinner and his Savior.
There was only a guilty man placing his hope in the crucified King.
And grace met him there.
That is the heart of Christianity.
Not the ability to reproduce Christ's appearance.
Not the possession of religious objects.
Not the superiority of one artistic tradition over another.
But salvation through Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
So what should Christians actually do about pictures of Jesus?
First, we must refuse idolatry without compromise.
No image should be treated as a god.
No object should be trusted as a source of divine power.
No painting should receive the worship owed to the Lord.
We must never believe that a particular image can guarantee protection, forgiveness, salvation, or access to God's favor.
And if any object becomes the focus of superstitious dependence, it must be rejected as such.
Second, we should be honest about what Scripture does and does not explicitly settle.
The Bible does not give us a photograph of Jesus or a direct New Testament command that resolves every modern question about portraits, films, children's illustrations, or devotional paintings.
Christians who reject all such representations appeal to serious biblical and theological arguments.

Christians who permit some representations also offer arguments they believe are consistent with Scripture, especially concerning the incarnation and the distinction between representation and worship.
We should examine those arguments carefully rather than pretending that centuries of disagreement can be dismissed with one slogan.
Third, we must respect the seriousness of conscience without making conscience a substitute for Scripture.
Romans 14 teaches important principles about acting in faith, avoiding contempt, and refusing to needlessly wound fellow believers in disputable matters.

That chapter does not establish that every question about images is merely a matter of preference. Whether a particular use of images is forbidden worship remains precisely the issue Christians must examine.
But it does warn us against arrogance.
A believer who is convinced that a representation of Jesus violates God's command should not violate that conviction.
And a believer who considers a non-worshipful illustration permissible should not assume that every Christian who disagrees is ignorant, hateful, or spiritually immature.
Love does not require us to abandon truth.
Truth does not authorize us to abandon love.
Fourth, we should ask whether our devotional practices actually lead us toward biblical faithfulness.
Does this artwork direct your attention toward the teachings of Christ?
Or has it become something you cannot imagine praying without?
Does it remind you of the Gospel?
Or have you begun attributing spiritual power to the object itself?
Are you using it as an illustration?
Or are you depending upon it in a way that belongs to God?
And perhaps most importantly, would you still seek Jesus with the same devotion if every picture disappeared tomorrow?
Because He is not confined to a frame.
He is not limited to a statue.
He is not dependent upon human imagination.
He is the living Lord.
And He has promised to be with His people.
There is a remarkable declaration in 1 Peter 1:8:
“Though you have not seen him, you love him.”
That is the beauty of Christian faith.
We have not seen His earthly face with our own eyes.
Yet we can truly love Him.
We have not touched His nail-scarred hands.
Yet we can trust the salvation accomplished through His wounds.
We have not stood physically beside His empty tomb.
Yet we can believe the apostolic testimony that He is risen.
And one day, those who belong to Him will see Him.
Revelation 22:4 declares:
“They will see his face.”
Think about that.
Not an imagined face.
Not a culturally adapted portrait.
Not a human attempt to capture divine beauty.
The face of the living Christ.
The Savior who was crucified.
The King who conquered death.
The Lord who knows His people by name.
Until that day, our faith must be anchored in His Word, not in our ability to visualize His appearance.
And our worship must be directed to God Himself.
Jesus said:
“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
— John 4:24, ESV
Spirit and truth.
Not merely atmosphere.
Not merely emotional intensity.
Not merely artistic beauty.
Not merely the absence of religious images.
Spirit and truth.
A church with magnificent artwork can be spiritually empty.
A church with bare walls can be spiritually empty.
A person who loves sacred paintings can be spiritually lost.
A person who rejects every sacred painting can be spiritually lost.
And a person from either setting can be genuinely redeemed through faith in Jesus Christ.
Because salvation is not determined by the decoration of the sanctuary.
It is found in Christ alone.
And that brings us to the question beneath every other question.
Have you surrendered to Him?
Not to a painting.
Not to a religious identity.
Not to a denomination.
Not to the approval of people who agree with your theology.
To Jesus.
The real Jesus.
The holy Jesus.
The merciful Jesus.
The Jesus who died for sins and rose again.
The Jesus who forgives and transforms those who turn to Him in faith.
Maybe you have spent years defending Christianity publicly while quietly losing your first love.
Maybe you have confused winning arguments with making disciples.
Maybe you have been so wounded by religious hypocrisy that even the name of Jesus now makes your heart ache.
Maybe you have been carrying shame for something nobody else knows.
And maybe tonight, you realize that you do not need another religious object to hold.
You need the Savior who holds fast to His people.
Come to Him.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what has enslaved you.
Trust His finished work on the cross.
Receive the grace that cannot be purchased, manufactured, or earned.
Because the most beautiful portrait of Jesus ever painted cannot forgive a single sin.
But Jesus Himself can.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a phrase.
The scandal is not simply that humanity has sometimes misrepresented God through religious imagery.
The deeper scandal is that sinful humanity rejected the very Son of God when He came among us.
He was mocked.
He was beaten.
He was crowned with thorns.
He was crucified.
And at the cross, the One who had committed no sin bore our sins, so that those who believe in Him might be reconciled to God (1 Peter 2:24; 2 Corinthians 5:21).
That is grace.
Not a sentimental painting.
Not a religious performance.
Not an emotional experience that fades by morning.
Grace written into history through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And if that truth has reached somewhere deep inside you, do not rush away from it.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to expose private sins publicly to prove your sincerity. God hears the confession you make to Him, even when nobody else knows the battle.
Someone reading your testimony may discover that they are not the only one wrestling with these questions.
Someone may finally open their Bible again.
Someone may be reminded that Christ is worthy of their trust.
And someone who has been watching Christians fight over religious symbols may finally encounter a conversation marked by both conviction and grace.
That is worth sharing.

Invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the person who has drifted from church, and even the person who does not yet believe. They deserve to encounter the Gospel itself, not merely arguments about Christianity.
And there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Behind every article, every devotional, every biblical resource, and every attempt to reach someone who feels spiritually forgotten is the ongoing work of making Christ known.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to those who may not be able to afford it.
We also want to be biblically careful here.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loves a cheerful giver.”
These products are not spiritual necessities. They are simply additional resources and everyday items through which supporters can engage with the ministry.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is helping someone understand Scripture.
It is encouraging a weary Christian to keep trusting Jesus.
It is pointing a searching soul toward repentance, forgiveness, and new life in Christ.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
And the Gospel must never become a transaction.
What we hope to build together is a community of believers who love God's Word more than religious appearances, who pursue holiness without pride, and who proclaim Christ without losing compassion.
Because the world does not simply need more pictures of Jesus.
It needs to hear the truth about Jesus.
It needs Christians who reflect His character in the way they live, forgive, serve, speak, and love.
And it needs the Gospel preached clearly enough that sinners can hear the call to repent and believe.
So whether your home contains religious paintings or no religious images at all, examine your heart before the Lord.
Let Scripture correct you.
Let the Holy Spirit convict you.
Let grace humble you.
And let the living Christ be the center of your worship.
Because when your final hour comes, you will not need a perfect portrait of His face.
You will need the Savior who died and rose again.
And when every picture has faded, every argument has fallen silent, and every earthly treasure has turned to dust, only one question will remain: Did you truly know the Jesus you claimed to worship?
